subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
"Dal or rajma tonight?"
"Rajma. It's Wednesday."
"Right. Wednesday." Sarita laughed. "Five years and we've turned into a timetable."
"A good timetable," Vijay said, eyes on the cricket score. "Did you pay the electricity bill?"
"Yesterday."
"You're the best."
She set the pressure cooker going. "I went to that pottery class on Saturday, you know. The trial one."
"Hmm? Nice. Was it nice?"
"It was... really nice. I've been thinking about it a lot."
"Good, good." He clapped as someone hit a six. "Oh, did Amma call you about Sunday?"
"She did."
Sarita stirred the rajma and didn't finish the sentence she'd started in her head: that she'd been thinking about more than pottery. About her job, about what she wanted. Vijay was lovely. He just hadn't asked in a long time. And she hadn't pushed.

qa.q: Why do they have rajma tonight?
qa.a: They have rajma because it's Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Sarita thinking about but didn't say?
qa.a: Sarita felt a little lonely, since Vijay hadn't asked in a long time, and had been thinking about more than pottery: her job and what she wants.

qa.q: What small change could help this couple keep knowing each other?
qa.a: Vijay could put the score aside and ask a real follow-up question, and Sarita could say what's on her mind instead of letting it drop.

qa.q: How might Vijay see their evening?
qa.a: Vijay likely sees a happy, easy routine and has no idea Sarita is holding back something important.

grounding: Shows a couple of five years in a warm routine where comfort has replaced curiosity, so a partner's inner changes go unasked and unspoken.

subtopic: A relationship's slow drift and breakup
passage:
I'm Lakshmi. Prakash and I have been married four years, and looking back at last year, I can see how comfortable we'd become. Filter coffee at seven, his cycling on Sundays, my mother's call at eight every night. It was easy. I liked easy.
What I didn't notice was how little we asked each other anything real. Prakash stopped mentioning his work around March. I assumed it was fine. My colleague Sangeeta asked once, "How's Prakash's new project?" and I realised I didn't even know he had one.
And I hadn't told him that I'd started dreading my own job. It didn't seem worth bringing up over coffee. We were so busy being comfortable that small changes slipped past, unannounced.
Nothing was wrong. That's what made it so easy to miss.

qa.q: When did Prakash stop mentioning his work?
qa.a: Prakash stopped mentioning his work around March.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi realise when Sangeeta asked about Prakash's project?
qa.a: Lakshmi was surprised to realise they had stopped asking each other about real things, and she didn't even know Prakash had a new project.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi and Prakash do to stay close within their routine?
qa.a: They could keep the comfortable rituals but add a real question now and then, like how work is truly going, and share worries such as Lakshmi's dread before they grow.

qa.q: How might Prakash have been feeling about his new project?
qa.a: Prakash may have been stressed or excited about it but didn't bring it up, perhaps thinking Lakshmi wasn't curious or that it could wait.

grounding: Illustrates a married couple's easy routine in which neither asks about the other's inner life, so changes at work go unspoken.
